title: Interior design
description: Design of interior spaces to benefit their occupants
wiki_lead: Interior design is the art and science of enhancing the interior of a building to achieve a healthier and more aesthetically pleasing environment for the people using the space. An interior designer is someone who plans, researches, coordinates, and manages such enhancement projects. Interior design is a multifaceted profession that includes conceptual development, space planning, site inspections, programming, research, communicating with the stakeholders of a project, construction management, and execution of the design. Interior designers make use of fundamental design principles from the visual arts used to help viewers understand a given scene.
wiki_excerpt:
Interior design is the art and science of enhancing the interior of a building to achieve a healthier and more aesthetically pleasing environment for the people using the space. An interior designer is someone who plans, researches, coordinates, and manages such enhancement projects. Interior design is a multifaceted profession that includes conceptual development, space planning, site inspections, programming, research, communicating with the stakeholders of a project, construction management, and execution of the design. Interior designers make use of fundamental design principles from the visual arts used to help viewers understand a given scene.


History and current terms

In the past, interiors were put together instinctively as a part of the process of building.
The profession of interior design has been a consequence of the development of society and the complex architecture that has resulted from the development of industrial processes.
The pursuit of effective use of space, user well-being and functional design has contributed to the development of the contemporary interior design profession. The profession of interior design is separate and distinct from the role of interior decorator, a term commonly used in the US; the term is less common in the UK, where the profession of interior design is still unregulated and therefore, strictly speaking, not yet officially a profession.
In ancient India, architects would also function as interior designers. This can be seen from the references of Vishwakarma the architect—one of the gods in Indian mythology. In these architects' design of 17th-century Indian homes, sculptures depicting ancient texts and events are seen inside the palaces, while during the medieval times wall art paintings were a common feature of palace-like mansions in India commonly known as havelis. While most traditional homes have been demolished to make way to modern buildings, there are still around 2000 havelis in the Shekhawati region of Rajasthan that display wall art paintings.
In ancient Egypt, "soul houses" (or models of houses) were placed in tombs as receptacles for food offerings. From these, it is possible to discern details about the interior design of different residences throughout the different Egyptian dynasties, such as changes in ventilation, porticoes, columns, loggias, windows, and doors.

Painting interior walls has existed for at least 5,000 years, with examples found as far north as the Ness of Brodgar, as have templated interiors, as seen in the associated Skara Brae settlement. It was the Greeks, and later Romans who added co-ordinated, decorative mosaics floors, and templated bath houses, shops, civil offices, Castra (forts) and temple, interiors, in the first millennia BC. With specialised guilds dedicated to producing interior decoration, and formulaic furniture, in buildings constructed to forms defined by Roman architects, such as Vitruvius: De architectura, libri decem (The Ten Books on Architecture).
Throughout the 17th and 18th century and into the early 19th century, interior decoration was the concern of the homemaker, or an employed upholsterer or craftsman who would advise on the artistic style for an interior space. Architects would also employ craftsmen or artisans to complete interior design for their buildings.


Commercial interior design and management
In the mid-to-late 19th century, interior design services expanded greatly, as the middle class in industrial countries grew in size and prosperity and began to desire the domestic trappings of wealth to cement their new status. Large furniture firms began to branch out into general interior design and management, offering full house furnishings in a variety of styles. This business model flourished from the mid-century to 1914, when this role was increasingly usurped by independent, often amateur, designers. This paved the way for the emergence of the professional interior design in the mid-20th century.

grok_lead: Interior design is the art and science of understanding people's behavior to create functional spaces within a building that are safe, aesthetically pleasing, and supportive of health and well-being. It encompasses a systematic methodology involving research, analysis, planning, and the integration of knowledge about human behavior, building codes, and environmental factors to enhance the quality of life for occupants. Unlike interior decorating, which focuses primarily on aesthetics and furnishings, interior design addresses the overall structure, functionality, and technical aspects of interior environments, often requiring formal education, experience, and certification such as the NCIDQ exam. The profession traces its roots to ancient civilizations, where Egyptians, Greeks, and Romans incorporated ornate murals, architectural elements, and personal furnishings into living spaces for religious, social, and practical purposes. In the early 20th century, interior design emerged as a distinct field from interior decoration, with the term "interior decorator" emerging in the early 1900s in America and formal courses introduced at institutions like the New York School of Applied and Fine Arts. Pioneers such as Elsie de Wolfe, who published The House in Good Taste in 1913, and Dorothy Draper, who founded the first commercial design firm in 1925, helped professionalize the discipline. By the 1930s, the term "interior designer" gained prominence, reflecting a shift toward technical expertise in health, safety, and welfare, leading to the formation of key organizations like the American Institute of Decorators in 1931, which merged with the National Society of Interior Designers to form the American Society of Interior Designers in 1975. Key aspects of interior design include determining space requirements, selecting materials and furnishings, ensuring compliance with building codes and accessibility standards like the Americans with Disabilities Act of 1992, and applying principles such as balance, proportion, rhythm, emphasis, scale, and harmony to create cohesive environments. Designers often specialize in areas like healthcare, where natural light and views can accelerate patient recovery, or sustainable design to minimize environmental impact while promoting occupant wellness. In the United States, the field employs about 87,100 professionals as of 2024, with a median annual wage of $63,490, and is projected to grow by 3% through 2034 due to ongoing demand for functional and innovative spaces.
